what_to_do: Get the full history of every RMB account, and of any other foreign-currency account you hold: each credit with its date, its amount and what it was.
why: The withdrawal method has to be applied to all accounts in a foreign currency, so all of them are needed.

what_to_do: Give each credit a dollar cost using the table 'What did your RMB cost in dollars?'. Take the rate for each date from one published source and keep to it; the Federal Reserve daily series is one.
why: The IRS accepts any posted rate used consistently, and the regulation names the Federal Reserve's rates.

what_to_do: Look at earlier U.S. returns for any earlier conversion. A method already used has to be kept. If there is none, choose first in first out, last in first out or pro rata now and write the choice down.
why: The method must be 'consistently applied from year to year'.

what_to_do: Write down what each part of the balance was for: living money, or money held to earn a return or for a business. That decides the box.
why: A transaction is personal except to the extent its costs would be business or income-producing expenses.

what_to_do: On each conversion day keep the bank's slip: RMB sold, the rate, dollars received.
why: The dollars received are the amount realized.

what_to_do: For each conversion on its own: gain or loss = dollars received − dollar cost of the RMB sold, by your method.

Apply the box. Investment or business: ordinary income or ordinary loss. Personal: a gain of $200 or less is ignored, a larger gain is a capital gain (long-term if held more than one year), a loss is not deductible.
why: These are the two sets of consequences in the statute and in IRS Publication 525.

what_to_do: Find your rate for that tax year in the bracket tables, and check whether your income passes the 3.8% threshold.
why: The tax is the gain placed on top of your other income for the year.

what_to_do: If you claim section 988 losses of $50,000 or more for the year, disclose the transaction on Form 8886. When and where to file it is in the form's instructions, which were not read.
why: A section 988 loss of that size is a reportable loss transaction for an individual, with a separate penalty for leaving it out.

what_to_do: Report it. A capital gain goes on Form 8949 and Schedule D. For an ordinary section 988 gain or loss, ask the preparer which line; this page could not confirm it from an official page.
why: Only the capital-gain route was found on an official page.
